> **Reproducibility note:** Place `credit_risk_dataset.csv` in the same folder as this `.Rmd` file before knitting. The data path is relative, so the report runs on any computer. All tables, numbers and plots are regenerated when the report is knitted; they are not copied from the notebook. Small differences from the originally reported figures are possible if package versions differ.

# Case Study Overview

## Problem statement

Loan default creates financial risk for lenders. This case study explores borrower and loan characteristics associated with default and builds predictive models in R to estimate whether a loan is likely to default.

## Objectives

- Clean and prepare the credit-risk dataset.
- Explore default patterns through tables and visualizations.
- Examine numerical correlations and categorical associations with loan status (chi-square tests).
- Train and evaluate Logistic Regression and Random Forest models on a stratified 80:20 train-test split.
- Compare the models using accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, ROC curves and AUC.
- Examine Random Forest feature importance.
- Run a probability-threshold experiment and a class-weighted Random Forest experiment.
- Use LIME to inspect one individual Random Forest prediction.

# Dataset

**Source:** Credit Risk Dataset on Kaggle - <https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/laotse/credit-risk-dataset>. The local file is `credit_risk_dataset.csv`.

The original file has 32,581 rows and 12 variables. The target is `loan_status`, where `0` denotes non-default and `1` denotes default.

| Variable | Description |
|---|---|
| `person_age` | Age of the borrower (years) |
| `person_income` | Annual income of the borrower |
| `person_home_ownership` | Home ownership status (RENT, OWN, MORTGAGE, OTHER) |
| `person_emp_length` | Employment length (years) |
| `loan_intent` | Purpose of the loan |
| `loan_grade` | Loan grade (A to G) |
| `loan_amnt` | Loan amount |
| `loan_int_rate` | Loan interest rate (%) |
| `loan_status` | Target: 0 = non-default, 1 = default |
| `loan_percent_income` | Loan amount as a fraction of income |
| `cb_person_default_on_file` | Historical default on file (Y/N) |
| `cb_person_cred_hist_length` | Credit history length (years) |

# Setup and Data Import

## Load required packages

All packages are loaded once, here, so every later chunk can rely on them.

```{r load-packages}
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(randomForest)
  library(caret)
  library(pROC)
  library(lime)
  library(dplyr)
  library(ggplot2)
  library(corrplot)
})

cat("All packages loaded successfully.\n")
```

```{r import-data}
file_path <- "credit_risk_dataset.csv"

if (!file.exists(file_path)) {

}
```

## Remove duplicates and invalid values

```{r cleaning}
# Start from the original dataset
loan_clean <- loan_data

# Remove exact duplicate rows
loan_clean <- loan_clean[!duplicated(loan_clean), ]

# Remove ages above 100
loan_clean <- loan_clean[loan_clean$person_age <= 100, ]

# Remove employment lengths above 50, keeping missing values
loan_clean <- loan_clean[
  is.na(loan_clean$person_emp_length) |
    loan_clean$person_emp_length <= 50,
]

cat("Cleaning completed.\n")
cat("Original rows:", nrow(loan_data), "\n")
cat("Cleaned rows:", nrow(loan_clean), "\n")
cat("Columns:", ncol(loan_clean), "\n")
```

## Verify the cleaned dataset

```{r verify-cleaning}

# Remaining missing values
colSums(is.na(loan_clean))

# Check age range
summary(loan_clean$person_age)

# Check employment length
summary(loan_clean$person_emp_length)

# Confirm no duplicate rows remain
sum(duplicated(loan_clean))
```

## Convert categorical variables into factors

The target `loan_status` is given the levels `"0"` and `"1"` here, and that order is used consistently in every later chunk.

```{r convert-factors}
loan_clean$person_home_ownership <- as.factor(loan_clean$person_home_ownership)
loan_clean$loan_intent           <- as.factor(loan_clean$loan_intent)
loan_clean$loan_grade            <- as.factor(loan_clean$loan_grade)
loan_clean$cb_person_default_on_file <- as.factor(loan_clean$cb_person_default_on_file)
loan_clean$loan_status           <- factor(loan_clean$loan_status, levels = c(0, 1))

str(loan_clean)
```

## Selected correlations among numerical variables

The notebook plotted an object called `correlations` without a visible definition. It is defined here from `cor_matrix` (computed above) for a set of variable pairs, so the plot always reflects the data. The pairs shown are the ones selected for this report.

```{r eda-selected-correlations}
selected_pairs <- data.frame(
  Var1 = c("person_age", "person_income", "loan_amnt",
           "person_income", "person_age", "loan_int_rate"),
  Var2 = c("cb_person_cred_hist_length", "loan_amnt", "loan_percent_income",
           "loan_percent_income", "person_emp_length", "loan_percent_income"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

correlations <- data.frame(
  Relationship = paste(selected_pairs$Var1, "vs", selected_pairs$Var2),
  Correlation  = unname(mapply(
    function(a, b) cor_matrix[a, b],
    selected_pairs$Var1, selected_pairs$Var2
  )),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE,
  row.names = NULL
)

correlations$Relationship <- factor(
  correlations$Relationship,
  levels = rev(correlations$Relationship)
)

print(correlations)

ggplot(correlations, aes(x = Relationship, y = Correlation)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_text(
    aes(
      label = sprintf("%.3f", Correlation),
      hjust = ifelse(Correlation < 0, 1.15, -0.15),
      color = Correlation < 0
    )
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c("TRUE" = "white", "FALSE" = "black"),
    guide = "none"
  ) +
  coord_flip(clip = "off") +
  scale_y_continuous(
    limits = c(-0.4, 1.0),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0.02, 0.12))
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Selected Correlations Among Numerical Variables",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Pearson Correlation (r)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(plot.margin = ggplot2::margin(10, 35, 10, 10))
```

# Statistical Analysis and Data Preparation

## Missing-value treatment: preliminary median imputation

Two variables contain missing values: `person_emp_length` and `loan_int_rate`. This chunk fills them with the **full-data** median on a separate copy (`loan_imputed`) so that descriptive statistics and the chi-square tests can use every row. It is **not** used for modelling: the models use training-set medians only (see the Logistic Regression section) to avoid information leaking from the test set.

```{r missing-values}
# Create a separate dataset for missing-value treatment
loan_imputed <- loan_clean

# Check missing values before treatment
cat("Missing values before treatment:\n")
print(colSums(is.na(loan_imputed)))

# 1. Fill missing employment length using the median
employment_median_all <- median(loan_imputed$person_emp_length, na.rm = TRUE)
loan_imputed$person_emp_length[is.na(loan_imputed$person_emp_length)] <-
  employment_median_all

# 2. Fill missing interest rate using the median
interest_median_all <- median(loan_imputed$loan_int_rate, na.rm = TRUE)
loan_imputed$loan_int_rate[is.na(loan_imputed$loan_int_rate)] <-
  interest_median_all

# Check missing values after treatment
cat("\nMissing values after treatment:\n")
print(colSums(is.na(loan_imputed)))

cat("\nDataset dimensions after imputation:\n")
print(dim(loan_imputed))

cat("\nMedian employment length used:", employment_median_all, "\n")
cat("Median interest rate used:", interest_median_all, "\n")
```

```{r missing-values-check}
# Confirm no missing values remain
stopifnot(sum(is.na(loan_imputed)) == 0)

# Confirm duplicate rows have not been introduced
cat("Duplicate rows:", sum(duplicated(loan_imputed)), "\n")

# Final structure
str(loan_imputed)

# Final summary
summary(loan_imputed)

cat("\nMissing-value treatment completed successfully.\n")
```

## Chi-square tests of association

Each categorical predictor is tested against `loan_status`. A small p-value indicates an association, not causation. Some cells (for example loan grade G and home ownership OTHER) are small, so those results should be read with care.

```{r chi-square}
# Variables to test against loan default
categorical_variables <- c(
  "loan_grade",
  "loan_intent",
  "person_home_ownership",
  "cb_person_default_on_file"
)

# Store results
chi_results <- data.frame(
  Variable = character(),
  Chi_Square = numeric(),
  Degrees_of_Freedom = integer(),
  P_Value = numeric(),
  Conclusion = character(),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

# Run each chi-square test
for (variable in categorical_variables) {

  contingency_table <- table(
    loan_imputed[[variable]],
    loan_imputed$loan_status
  )

  test_result <- chisq.test(contingency_table)

  conclusion <- if (test_result$p.value < 0.05) {
    "Statistically significant association"
  } else {
    "No statistically significant association"
  }

  chi_results <- rbind(
    chi_results,
    data.frame(
      Variable = variable,
      Chi_Square = unname(test_result$statistic),
      Degrees_of_Freedom = unname(test_result$parameter),
      P_Value = test_result$p.value,
      Conclusion = conclusion,
      stringsAsFactors = FALSE
    )
  )
}

# Display results
chi_results$Chi_Square <- round(chi_results$Chi_Square, 3)
chi_results$P_Value <- signif(chi_results$P_Value, 4)

print(chi_results, row.names = FALSE)
```

## Train-test split: 80:20 stratified sampling

The split is made on `loan_clean` (before any imputation), so no test-set information is used to fill missing values.

```{r train-test-split}
model_data <- loan_clean

# Ensure target has the correct class order
model_data$loan_status <- factor(model_data$loan_status, levels = c("0", "1"))

# Reproducible 80:20 stratified split
set.seed(123)

train_index <- createDataPartition(
  model_data$loan_status,
  p = 0.80,
  list = FALSE
)

train_data <- model_data[train_index, ]
test_data  <- model_data[-train_index, ]

# Verify split
cat("Training rows:", nrow(train_data), "\n")
cat("Testing rows:", nrow(test_data), "\n")

cat("\nTraining target distribution (%):\n")
print(round(prop.table(table(train_data$loan_status)) * 100, 2))

cat("\nTesting target distribution (%):\n")
print(round(prop.table(table(test_data$loan_status)) * 100, 2))

cat("\nTrain/test split completed.\n")
```

# Machine Learning Models

## Prepare data and train Logistic Regression

Missing values are filled with medians calculated from the **training** data only, and the same values are applied to the test data.

```{r logistic-train}
# 1. Calculate imputation values from training data only
employment_median <- median(train_data$person_emp_length, na.rm = TRUE)
interest_median   <- median(train_data$loan_int_rate, na.rm = TRUE)

# 2. Apply the training medians to both datasets
train_data$person_emp_length[is.na(train_data$person_emp_length)] <- employment_median
test_data$person_emp_length[is.na(test_data$person_emp_length)]    <- employment_median

train_data$loan_int_rate[is.na(train_data$loan_int_rate)] <- interest_median
test_data$loan_int_rate[is.na(test_data$loan_int_rate)]    <- interest_median

# 3. Train Logistic Regression (all other columns are predictors)
logistic_model <- glm(
  loan_status ~ .,
  data = train_data,
  family = binomial(link = "logit")
)

# 4. Display model results
summary(logistic_model)

cat("\nLogistic Regression training completed.\n")
cat("Training rows:", nrow(train_data), "\n")
cat("Testing rows:", nrow(test_data), "\n")
cat("Remaining missing values in training data:", sum(is.na(train_data)), "\n")
cat("Remaining missing values in testing data:", sum(is.na(test_data)), "\n")
```

## Evaluate Logistic Regression on test data

`actual_status` and `conf_matrix` are created first, and the confusion-matrix plot and metrics are built from them. In the confusion table, rows are predictions and columns are actual classes, with `"1"` (default) as the positive class.

```{r logistic-evaluate}
# Predict probability of default (loan_status = 1)
logistic_prob <- predict(logistic_model, newdata = test_data, type = "response")

# Convert probabilities into class predictions using a 0.5 threshold
logistic_pred <- factor(ifelse(logistic_prob >= 0.5, "1", "0"), levels = c("0", "1"))

# Actual classes for the test set (used by every later evaluation)
actual_status <- factor(test_data$loan_status, levels = c("0", "1"))

# Confusion matrix (created BEFORE it is plotted or used for metrics)
conf_matrix <- confusionMatrix(
  data = logistic_pred,
  reference = actual_status,
  positive = "1"
)

# Visual confusion matrix - Logistic Regression
logistic_cm_df <- as.data.frame(conf_matrix$table)
colnames(logistic_cm_df) <- c("Predicted", "Actual", "Count")

ggplot(logistic_cm_df, aes(x = Actual, y = Predicted, fill = Count)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 1.5) +
  geom_text(aes(label = Count), size = 8, fontface = "bold") +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#DCEBFA", high = "#245A9C") +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = c("0" = "Non-Default", "1" = "Default")) +
  scale_y_discrete(labels = c("0" = "Non-Default", "1" = "Default")) +
  labs(
    title = "Confusion Matrix - Logistic Regression",
    subtitle = "Test Dataset",
    x = "Actual Class",
    y = "Predicted Class",
    fill = "Count"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0.5),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(hjust = 0.5),
    axis.text = element_text(face = "bold"),
    panel.grid = element_blank()
  )

# Calculate evaluation metrics
cm <- conf_matrix$table

true_negative  <- cm["0", "0"]
false_negative <- cm["0", "1"]
false_positive <- cm["1", "0"]
true_positive  <- cm["1", "1"]

accuracy  <- (true_positive + true_negative) / sum(cm)
precision <- ifelse(
  true_positive + false_positive > 0,
  true_positive / (true_positive + false_positive), 0
)
recall <- ifelse(
  true_positive + false_negative > 0,
  true_positive / (true_positive + false_negative), 0
)
f1_score <- ifelse(
  precision + recall > 0,
  2 * precision * recall / (precision + recall), 0
)

cat("\n--- Logistic Regression Test Metrics ---\n")
cat("Accuracy :", round(accuracy, 4), "\n")
cat("Precision:", round(precision, 4), "\n")
cat("Recall   :", round(recall, 4), "\n")
cat("F1-score :", round(f1_score, 4), "\n")
```

## ROC curve and AUC: Logistic Regression

```{r logistic-roc}
roc_result <- roc(
  response = actual_status,
  predictor = logistic_prob,
  levels = c("0", "1"),
  direction = "<",
  quiet = TRUE
)

auc_value <- as.numeric(auc(roc_result))

cat("Logistic Regression ROC-AUC:", round(auc_value, 4), "\n")

plot(roc_result, main = "ROC Curve - Logistic Regression", col = "blue", lwd = 2)
abline(a = 0, b = 1, lty = 2, col = "red")
```

## Train the Random Forest model

```{r rf-train}
set.seed(123)

rf_model <- randomForest(
  loan_status ~ .,
  data = train_data,
  ntree = 300,
  importance = TRUE
)

print(rf_model)

cat("\nRandom Forest training completed.\n")
```

## Evaluate Random Forest on test data

As with Logistic Regression, `rf_conf_matrix` is created before it is plotted or used for metrics. The predicted classes (`rf_pred`) come from the forest's majority vote, which can differ very slightly from applying a 0.50 cut-off to `rf_prob` (this is why the threshold table later shows a tiny difference at 0.50).

```{r rf-evaluate}
# Predicted probability of default and predicted class
rf_prob <- predict(rf_model, newdata = test_data, type = "prob")[, "1"]
rf_pred <- factor(
  as.character(predict(rf_model, newdata = test_data, type = "response")),
  levels = c("0", "1")
)

# Confusion matrix (created BEFORE it is plotted or used for metrics)
rf_conf_matrix <- confusionMatrix(
  data = rf_pred,
  reference = actual_status,
  positive = "1"
)

# Visual confusion matrix - Random Forest
rf_cm_df <- as.data.frame(rf_conf_matrix$table)
colnames(rf_cm_df) <- c("Predicted", "Actual", "Count")

ggplot(rf_cm_df, aes(x = Actual, y = Predicted, fill = Count)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 1.5) +
  geom_text(aes(label = Count), size = 8, fontface = "bold") +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#DCEBFA", high = "#245A9C") +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = c("0" = "Non-Default", "1" = "Default")) +
  scale_y_discrete(labels = c("0" = "Non-Default", "1" = "Default")) +
  labs(
    title = "Confusion Matrix - Random Forest",
    subtitle = "Test Dataset",
    x = "Actual Class",
    y = "Predicted Class",
    fill = "Count"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0.5),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(hjust = 0.5),
    axis.text = element_text(face = "bold"),
    panel.grid = element_blank()
  )

rf_cm <- rf_conf_matrix$table

rf_tn <- rf_cm["0", "0"]
rf_fn <- rf_cm["0", "1"]
rf_fp <- rf_cm["1", "0"]
rf_tp <- rf_cm["1", "1"]

rf_accuracy  <- (rf_tp + rf_tn) / sum(rf_cm)
rf_precision <- rf_tp / (rf_tp + rf_fp)
rf_recall    <- rf_tp / (rf_tp + rf_fn)
rf_f1        <- 2 * rf_precision * rf_recall / (rf_precision + rf_recall)

cat("\n--- Random Forest Test Metrics ---\n")
cat("Accuracy :", round(rf_accuracy, 4), "\n")
cat("Precision:", round(rf_precision, 4), "\n")
cat("Recall   :", round(rf_recall, 4), "\n")
cat("F1-score :", round(rf_f1, 4), "\n")

rf_roc <- roc(
  response = actual_status,
  predictor = rf_prob,
  levels = c("0", "1"),
  direction = "<",
  quiet = TRUE
)

rf_auc <- as.numeric(auc(rf_roc))
cat("ROC-AUC  :", round(rf_auc, 4), "\n")

plot(rf_roc, main = "ROC Curve - Random Forest", col = "blue", lwd = 2)
abline(a = 0, b = 1, lty = 2, col = "red")
```

## Model performance comparison

```{r model-comparison}

  F1_Score  = c(f1_score, rf_f1),

print(comparison_print, row.names = FALSE)

plot(rf_roc, col = "firebrick", lwd = 2, add = TRUE)
abline(a = 0, b = 1, lty = 2, col = "grey40")
legend(
  "bottomright",
  legend = c(
    paste0("Logistic Regression (AUC = ", round(auc_value, 4), ")"),
    paste0("Random Forest (AUC = ", round(rf_auc, 4), ")")

)
```

# Experiments

## Random Forest threshold-tuning experiment

The default decision threshold is 0.50. Lowering it flags more loans as defaults, which usually raises recall and lowers precision.

```{r threshold-tuning}
thresholds <- c(0.50, 0.45, 0.40, 0.35, 0.30, 0.25, 0.20)

threshold_results <- data.frame()

for (threshold in thresholds) {

  pred <- factor(
    ifelse(rf_prob >= threshold, "1", "0"),
    levels = c("0", "1")
  )

  cm_t <- confusionMatrix(
    data = pred,
    reference = actual_status,
    positive = "1"
  )

  threshold_results <- rbind(
    threshold_results,
    data.frame(
      Threshold = threshold,
      Accuracy  = unname(cm_t$overall["Accuracy"]),
      Precision = unname(cm_t$byClass["Pos Pred Value"]),
      Recall    = unname(cm_t$byClass["Sensitivity"]),
      F1        = unname(cm_t$byClass["F1"])
    )
  )
}

print(round(threshold_results, 4), row.names = FALSE)

# Visualize recall and precision trade-off
threshold_plot <- rbind(
  data.frame(
    Threshold = threshold_results$Threshold,
    Metric = "Recall",
    Value = threshold_results$Recall
  ),
  data.frame(
    Threshold = threshold_results$Threshold,
    Metric = "Precision",
    Value = threshold_results$Precision
  )
)

ggplot(threshold_plot, aes(x = Threshold, y = Value, color = Metric)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  scale_x_reverse(breaks = thresholds) +
  labs(
    title = "Random Forest: Threshold Tuning",
    x = "Probability Threshold",
    y = "Score",
    color = "Metric"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)
```

> **Limitation:** the threshold of 0.40 was chosen after looking at the **test-set** results above. The 0.40 figures are therefore an experiment, not an unbiased estimate of future performance. A stricter design would choose the threshold on a separate validation set and evaluate it once on an untouched test set.

# LIME Explainability

LIME fits a simple local model around one test applicant to show which feature ranges pushed the Random Forest towards "default" for that case. Two small S3 methods tell `lime` how to treat a `randomForest` model and how to obtain class probabilities (columns named `"0"` and `"1"`). A seed is set so the explanation can be repeated; LIME samples randomly, so the numbers can still differ slightly between package versions.


```{r lime-explain}
# Tell lime how to handle a randomForest classification model
model_type.randomForest <- function(x, ...) {
  "classification"
}

predict_model.randomForest <- function(x, newdata, type, ...) {
  probabilities <- predict(x, newdata = newdata, type = "prob")
  as.data.frame(probabilities, check.names = FALSE)
}

# Register methods for the lime package
registerS3method(
  "model_type",
  "randomForest",
  model_type.randomForest,
  envir = asNamespace("lime")
)

registerS3method(
  "predict_model",
  "randomForest",
  predict_model.randomForest,
  envir = asNamespace("lime")
)

# Prepare training features (exclude target)
lime_train <- train_data[
  , setdiff(names(train_data), "loan_status"),
  drop = FALSE
]

# Create LIME explainer
lime_explainer <- lime::lime(
  x = lime_train,
  model = rf_model,
  bin_continuous = TRUE,
  n_bins = 4,
  quantile_bins = TRUE
)

# Select the first test applicant predicted as default
default_cases <- which(as.character(rf_pred) == "1")

if (length(default_cases) == 0) {
  stop("No applicants predicted as default. Check rf_pred.")
}

case_index <- default_cases[1]

# Extract applicant features (exclude target)
applicant <- test_data[
  case_index,
  setdiff(names(test_data), "loan_status"),
  drop = FALSE
]

# Check predicted class probabilities
check_probs <- predict_model.randomForest(
  rf_model,
  applicant,
  type = "prob"
)

print(check_probs)

if (!all(c("0", "1") %in% names(check_probs))) {
  stop("Expected probability columns named '0' and '1'.")
}

# Generate LIME explanation for the default class
set.seed(123)

lime_explanation <- lime::explain(
  x = applicant,
  explainer = lime_explainer,
  n_features = 6,
  labels = "1"
)

# Display explanation results
lime_results <- as.data.frame(lime_explanation)

print(
  lime_results[
    ,
    c(
      "feature",
      "feature_value",
      "feature_desc",
      "feature_weight",
      "label_prob",
      "model_r2"
    ),
    drop = FALSE
  ]
)

# Plot influential features
plot_features(lime_explanation)

# Display prediction and actual outcome
cat("Applicant index:", case_index, "\n")
cat("Predicted class:", as.character(rf_pred[case_index]), "\n")
cat("Actual class:", as.character(actual_status[case_index]), "\n")
```


The original run reported a model probability of about 0.88 for this case and a LIME explanation fit (`model_r2`) of about 0.14, which is low. A low fit means the local linear model explains little of the forest's behaviour around this applicant, so the individual feature contributions should be read cautiously.

# Conclusion

**Data preparation.** The original file has 32,581 rows and 12 variables. After removing 165 duplicate rows and a few invalid records (ages above 100 and employment lengths above 50 years), 32,409 rows remain. Default cases make up 7,088 rows (21.87%), so the classes are imbalanced. A stratified 80:20 split gives 25,928 training and 6,481 test records, and missing values in the models are filled with training-set medians.

**Exploratory and statistical findings.** Default rates differ across loan grades, loan purposes, home-ownership groups and previous-default history, and the chi-square tests found a statistically significant association between each categorical variable and loan status. These are associations, not causal relationships.

**Baseline model comparison (reported results).**

| Model | Accuracy | Precision | Recall | F1-score | ROC-AUC |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Logistic Regression | 86.19% | 75.54% | 54.48% | 0.6330 | 0.8639 |
| Random Forest (threshold 0.50) | 93.75% | 97.65% | 73.18% | 0.8366 | 0.9384 |

Random Forest outperformed Logistic Regression on every reported metric.

**Threshold-tuning experiment.** At a threshold of 0.40 the Random Forest reported 93.64% accuracy, 94.67% precision, 75.16% recall, an F1-score of 0.8379 and 86.99% balanced accuracy (confusion matrix: TN = 5,004, FP = 60, FN = 352, TP = 1,065). Compared with 0.50, it catches more defaults at the cost of more false positives. The 0.40 threshold was selected after examining test-set results, so this is an experiment rather than an unbiased final estimate.

**Class-weighted Random Forest.** Giving the default class a weight of 2 did not improve recall in the reported run (about 72.6% versus 73.2% at the baseline).

**LIME.** LIME was applied to one test applicant who was predicted as default and was an actual default. Its explanation fit was low, so the explanation is only indicative.

## Limitations and future work

- Default cases are about 21.87% of the cleaned data, so class imbalance remains relevant.
- Loan grade G contains 64 records and the `OTHER` home-ownership group contains 106 records; findings for these small groups need caution.
- Threshold selection used the test set; it should be done on a validation set in future work.
- Associations, feature importance and LIME explanations do not establish causal root causes.
- The LIME example had a low explanation fit.
- Results depend on this dataset and one random split, and may not generalise to other lending populations or time periods.
- Future work: validation-based threshold selection, cross-validation, other imbalance-handling methods, and testing on new data.

# Reproducibility Instructions

1. Download or clone the project folder so that `Loan_Default_Risk_Analysis_Final.Rmd` and `credit_risk_dataset.csv` are in the **same folder**.
2. Open `Loan_Default_Risk_Analysis_Final.Rmd` in RStudio.
3. Make sure these R packages are installed (the first chunk installs any that are missing, which needs an internet connection): `dplyr`, `ggplot2`, `corrplot`, `caret`, `pROC`, `randomForest`, `lime`.
4. Click **Knit > Knit to HTML**. The output `Loan_Default_Risk_Analysis_Final.html` is created next to the `.Rmd` file.
5. Random seeds are fixed (`set.seed(123)`) before the train-test split, each Random Forest and the LIME explanation, so a re-run with the same R and package versions should reproduce the same results. Training the two Random Forests can take a few minutes.
